scenes.heading: Old triangle, new shape
scenes.text: The fire triangle had three sides. The fire tetrahedron adds a fourth: the chemical chain reaction.

scenes.heading: Fuel
scenes.text: Fuel is anything that burns. Solid, liquid or gas. Remove it, like shutting a gas valve, and the fire starves.

scenes.heading: Heat
scenes.text: Heat raises fuel to ignition temperature. Water absorbs heat. Cooling is why a fog or straight stream works.

scenes.heading: Oxygen and chain reaction
scenes.text: Fire needs oxygen, about 16 percent or more to flame. Break the chain reaction with dry chemical or clean agents.

scenes.heading: Memory hook
scenes.text: F-H-O-C: Fuel, Heat, Oxygen, Chain reaction. Pull ANY one leg of the tetrahedron and the fire goes out.

quiz.q: What is the fourth side of the fire tetrahedron?
quiz.explain: The tetrahedron adds an uninhibited chemical chain reaction to fuel, heat and oxygen.

quiz.q: Which method extinguishes fire by removing heat?
quiz.explain: Water absorbs heat, cooling fuel below ignition temperature.

scenes.heading: Incipient
scenes.text: Stage one: small fire, limited to the first fuel. Best time for an extinguisher or a quick attack.

scenes.heading: Growth
scenes.text: Fire grows, plume rises, hot gas layer banks down from the ceiling. Temperatures climb fast.

scenes.heading: Flashover
scenes.text: Transition where everything in the room ignites at once. Rollover, heat banking down and rapid temp rise warn you.

scenes.heading: Fully developed, then decay
scenes.text: Flashover leads to fully developed burning. Later, fuel or oxygen runs low and the fire decays.

scenes.heading: Memory hook
scenes.text: I-G-F-D: Incipient, Growth, Fully developed, Decay. Flashover is the bridge from growth to fully developed.

quiz.q: Which is a flashover warning sign?
choices: Rollover in the hot gas layer
Clear air at the floor only
quiz.explain: Rollover, heat banking down and rapidly rising temperatures warn of flashover.

quiz.q: Flashover happens between which stages?
quiz.explain: Flashover is the transition from growth to fully developed burning.

scenes.heading: What it is
scenes.text: Backdraft is an explosive ignition when oxygen suddenly enters a hot, oxygen-starved space full of unburned gases.

scenes.heading: Look outside first
scenes.text: Signs: smoke-stained windows, little visible flame, hot doors and glass. Smoke pushing out then pulling back in.

scenes.heading: Pulsing smoke
scenes.text: Puffing, pulsing smoke at gaps and a whistling sound as air is drawn in are classic indicators.

scenes.heading: Cool before you open
scenes.text: Vent vertically at the top first so gases escape. Coordinate with the crew and stay low and out of the door line.

scenes.heading: Memory hook
scenes.text: Hot glass, pulsing smoke, little flame, whistle in. If the building is breathing, do NOT swing open the door.

quiz.q: What triggers a backdraft?
choices: Adding oxygen to a starved, superheated space
quiz.explain: Sudden oxygen entry to hot unburned gases causes explosive ignition.

quiz.q: Which is a backdraft sign?
choices: Pulsing smoke with air drawn in
quiz.explain: Pulsing smoke and air being pulled in indicate a possible backdraft.

scenes.heading: A and B
scenes.text: Class A: ordinary combustibles like wood and paper. Class B: flammable liquids and gases like gasoline.

scenes.heading: C and D
scenes.text: Class C: energized electrical equipment. Class D: combustible metals like magnesium and titanium.

scenes.heading: Class K
scenes.text: Class K: cooking oils and fats in commercial kitchens. Wet chemical agents are used for these fires.

scenes.heading: PASS it
scenes.text: Pull the pin, Aim at the base, Squeeze the handle, Sweep side to side. Stay a safe distance.

scenes.heading: Memory hook
scenes.text: A=Ash, B=Barrel (liquids), C=Current, D=Dangerous metals (magnesium, sodium), K=Kitchen. Then PASS: Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep.

quiz.q: Which class covers cooking oils and fats?
quiz.explain: Class K fires involve cooking oils and fats.

quiz.q: In PASS, what does the A stand for?
quiz.explain: Aim the extinguisher at the base of the fire.

scenes.heading: Check before you go
scenes.text: Inspect cylinder pressure, regulator, harness and facepiece seal. Do it at shift start, every time.

scenes.heading: Donning methods
scenes.text: Over-the-head, coat method, seat-mounted. Tighten straps, seal facepiece and check for leaks before entering.

scenes.heading: Low-air alarm
scenes.text: The low-air alarm activates at 25 percent of cylinder capacity. Leave when it sounds, not after.

scenes.heading: Rule of thirds
scenes.text: Plan air use: one third to go in, one third to get out, one third reserve. Know your consumption.

scenes.heading: Memory hook
scenes.text: Alarm at a quarter, exit at a third. Your air is your lifeline, and nobody else is going to watch your gauge.

quiz.q: At what cylinder level does the low-air alarm activate?
quiz.explain: The low-air alarm activates at 25 percent of cylinder capacity.

quiz.q: Under the rule of thirds, one third of air is used for what?
quiz.explain: One third is going in, one third out, one third reserve.

scenes.heading: Call it early
scenes.text: Lost, trapped, out of air or injured? Call Mayday immediately. Delay kills. Say it three times.

scenes.heading: Say it clearly
scenes.text: Key the radio and say, Mayday, Mayday, Mayday. Command will clear the channel and ask for your info.

scenes.heading: LUNAR report
scenes.text: Give Location, Unit, Name, Assignment, Resources needed. Short and clear.

scenes.heading: Make noise
scenes.text: Activate your PASS device and use a flashlight, tool tapping and voice so rescuers can find you.

scenes.heading: Memory hook
scenes.text: LUNAR: Location, Unit, Name, Assignment, Resources. A mayday is no time to be embarrassed, make the call.

quiz.q: What does the R in LUNAR stand for?
quiz.explain: LUNAR: Location, Unit, Name, Assignment, Resources needed.

quiz.q: How many times do you say Mayday at first call?
quiz.explain: Say Mayday three times to get priority attention.

scenes.heading: The standard
scenes.text: NFPA 1971 covers structural firefighting protective ensembles: coat, pants, helmet, gloves, boots and hood.

scenes.heading: Three layers
scenes.text: Coat and pants have an outer shell, a moisture barrier and a thermal liner. Layers trap insulating air.

scenes.heading: No skin showing
scenes.text: Hood closes the gap between helmet, collar and facepiece. Gloves overlap coat sleeves. Cover everything.

scenes.heading: Care counts
scenes.text: Dirty or damaged gear loses protection. NFPA 1851 covers inspection, cleaning and repair. Clean after fires.

scenes.heading: Memory hook
scenes.text: 1971 is for the gear, 1981 is for SCBA. Three layers: shell, barrier, liner. Wear all of it, all the time.

quiz.q: Which NFPA standard covers structural firefighting protective ensembles?
quiz.explain: NFPA 1971 sets requirements for structural firefighting ensembles.

quiz.q: Which is a layer of turnout coats?
quiz.explain: Turnout gear has an outer shell, moisture barrier and thermal liner.

scenes.heading: The magic angle
scenes.text: A properly placed ground ladder sits at about 75 degrees. Strong, stable and good for climbing.

scenes.heading: The 4:1 rule
scenes.text: Place the base one foot away from the wall for every four feet of working height.

scenes.heading: Roof access
scenes.text: For roof access, extend the ladder tip at least three rungs above the roofline so you can step on and off.

scenes.heading: Safe footing
scenes.text: Lock halyard or pawls, level the base, check for wires, and always have a firefighter foot the ladder.

scenes.heading: Memory hook
scenes.text: 75 and 4:1. One foot out per four feet up, and three rungs above the roof. Easy.

quiz.q: What is the proper placement angle for a ground ladder?
quiz.explain: Ground ladders are placed at about 75 degrees.

quiz.q: Under the 4:1 rule, how far out for 20 feet of working height?
quiz.explain: 20 divided by 4 is 5 feet from the wall.

scenes.heading: Hose sizes
scenes.text: Attack lines are often 1 3/4 inch. Larger handlines are 2 1/2 inch. Large-diameter hose supplies water.

scenes.heading: GPM matters
scenes.text: Flow is measured in gallons per minute. A 1 3/4 inch line commonly flows roughly 150 to 200 GPM.

scenes.heading: Smooth bore
scenes.text: Smooth bore nozzles run around 50 psi at the nozzle for handlines. Reach is solid and penetrating.

scenes.heading: Fog nozzle
scenes.text: Fog nozzles often operate at 100 psi and can adjust pattern from straight stream to wide fog.

scenes.heading: Memory hook
scenes.text: Smooth bore: 50 psi. Fog: 100 psi. Big pipe, big GPM, big nozzle reaction. Brace and bleed air first.

quiz.q: What nozzle pressure is typical for a handline smooth bore nozzle?
quiz.explain: Handline smooth bore nozzles are commonly operated at 50 psi.

quiz.q: What does GPM measure?
quiz.explain: GPM is gallons per minute, the flow rate.

scenes.heading: Type I
scenes.text: Type I is fire resistive: concrete and protected steel. Highest resistance to collapse.

scenes.heading: Type II
scenes.text: Type II is noncombustible: unprotected metal and masonry. Steel can fail fast in fire.

scenes.heading: Type III
scenes.text: Type III is ordinary construction: masonry exterior walls with wood floors and roof. Watch for hidden voids.

scenes.heading: Type IV and V
scenes.text: Type IV is heavy timber with large wood members. Type V is wood frame, like most houses.

scenes.heading: Memory hook
scenes.text: I Fire-resistive, II Noncombustible, III Ordinary, IV Heavy timber, V Wood frame. Fiery Nachos Offer Hot Wings.

quiz.q: Which type is wood frame construction?
quiz.explain: Type V is wood frame, commonly found in houses.

quiz.q: Type III ordinary construction has what feature?
quiz.explain: Ordinary construction has masonry exterior walls and wood interior elements.

scenes.heading: Fire follows air
scenes.text: Fire moves toward fresh air. The flow path runs from inlets to exhaust openings, and the fire follows it.

scenes.heading: Doors are tools
scenes.text: Closed doors limit air and slow fire growth. Control doors when you can, and close them behind you.

scenes.heading: Coordinate vent
scenes.text: Ventilation without a hoseline ready can make fire grow. Time vent with attack and stay out of the flow path.

scenes.heading: Vertical or horizontal
scenes.text: Vertical ventilation uses roof openings. Horizontal uses windows and doors, sometimes with fans like PPV.

scenes.heading: Memory hook
scenes.text: Fire follows air. Coordinate, cool, then vent. Never vent without a plan and a hoseline.

quiz.q: What is the flow path?
quiz.explain: Flow path runs from inlet openings to exhaust openings.

quiz.q: Why coordinate ventilation with attack?
quiz.explain: Adding air can intensify fire, so vent with a hoseline ready.

scenes.heading: Primary search
scenes.text: Primary search is a quick but thorough search for victims, done first, with the fire attack in progress.

scenes.heading: Oriented search
scenes.text: Teams stay oriented using a wall, hoseline, rope or a thermal imager. Keep contact with each other.

scenes.heading: VES
scenes.text: Vent, Enter, Search: vent a window from outside, enter, search the room, and close the door behind you.

scenes.heading: RIT ready
scenes.text: Two-in, two-out applies in IDLH atmospheres. A rapid intervention team stands ready to rescue downed firefighters.

scenes.heading: Memory hook
scenes.text: VES: Vent, Enter, Search. RIT: Ready Is Required. Stay with your crew and know your way out.

quiz.q: What does VES stand for?
quiz.explain: VES is Vent, Enter, Search.

quiz.q: What does a RIT do?
quiz.explain: The rapid intervention team is ready to rescue firefighters in trouble.
